real_qa.q: What was Rebecca Bultsma's background before becoming an AI ethicist?
real_qa.r: Rebecca Bultsma worked in PR and communications before transitioning to AI ethics. When ChatGPT came out, she realized her PR skills were directly transferable to working with AI tools, as effective communication and clear instruction-giving were essential to using these systems well. This realization prompted her to enroll in a master's program at the University of Edinburgh about three years ago to understand the technology's implications.

real_qa.q: What does Rebecca Bultsma identify as the biggest mistake business leaders make with AI?
real_qa.r: Rebecca Bultsma states that replacing people is the biggest mistake. Early companies announced they were AI-first and had replaced 30% of their workforce with AI, but all of those companies had to hire people back. She emphasizes that the best approach is investing in teams' AI learning to help them build capacity, become better employees, and create better output while being happier, as AI cannot replicate what people do.
real_qa.requete: biggest mistake business leaders AI replacement

real_qa.q: According to Rebecca Bultsma, what human skills will become more valuable with AI in the workplace?
real_qa.r: Rebecca Bultsma emphasizes that communication, collaboration, and the ability to be an orchestrator of multiple AI agents will become critical. She stresses that curiosity and willingness to experiment are the most important skills to develop, as leaders must facilitate this mindset. These foundational human qualities, combined with the ability to prioritize tasks and determine where AI is useful versus where human judgment is needed, will distinguish valuable employees.

real_qa.q: What does Rebecca Bultsma recommend for using AI in professional communications and marketing?
real_qa.r: Rebecca Bultsma recommends using AI backstage rather than in direct customer-facing work. She advises thinking small and focusing on what Anthropic called the paper cuts of life—tedious, repetitive tasks. She suggests using AI to challenge and stress-test thinking, spot gaps, provide counter-arguments, and help see blind spots, rather than having it generate final public-facing content, which should always be human-vetted and attributed.

real_qa.q: Why did New York City and LA school districts ban AI for students under grade nine according to Rebecca Bultsma?
real_qa.r: Rebecca Bultsma states that New York City public schools and LA school districts banned student-facing AI for children younger than grade nine, though teachers can still use it. She supports this ban because she has found no evidence in the research space that student-facing AI is beneficial for student learning. She advocates for returning to basics in classrooms with less screen time and more focus on teaching curiosity, collaboration, communication, and oral skills.
real_qa.requete: New York City LA schools ban AI grade nine

guest.bio_context: Rebecca Bultsma transitioned from a PR and communications background to AI ethics after experimenting with ChatGPT upon its release. She enrolled in a master's program at the University of Edinburgh approximately three years ago to deeply understand the implications of AI technology. She now travels globally speaking about AI ethics and runs her own consultancy, working with executive leadership teams, K-12 education, and university presidents across multiple sectors.
